specPoints.text: know the general rules for predicting the solubility of ionic compounds in water: common sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds are soluble; all nitrates are soluble; common chlorides are soluble, except those of silver and lead(II); common sulfates are soluble, except for those of barium, calcium and lead(II); common carbonates are insoluble, except for those of sodium, potassium and ammonium; common hydroxides are insoluble except for those of sodium, potassium and calcium (calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble)

primer.text: From Ionic Bonding you know that ionic compounds are built from charged particles held in a lattice. Whether such a compound dissolves in water decides how its salts can be prepared in the laboratory. This note sets out the solubility rules of record, the famous exceptions, and why limewater matters.

lessons.title: Solubility rules
lessons.opening: Ionic compounds are generally more soluble in water than covalent substances, but the pattern has firm exceptions worth memorising. Every common salt of sodium, potassium and ammonium dissolves, and so do all nitrates. Beyond those families, most chlorides and sulfates dissolve while most carbonates and hydroxides do not, and knowing which is which tells you the right way to make any required salt.
keyPoints: All common sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble.
Most chlorides and sulfates are soluble in water.
Most carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble.
Solubility knowledge decides the most appropriate method for preparing a salt.

low.restatement: Three families always dissolve: sodium, potassium and ammonium salts, plus every nitrate. Most chlorides and sulfates dissolve too, while most carbonates and hydroxides stay out of solution.
low.analogy: Think of guests at a party: three families always come, meaning the sodium-potassium-ammonium salts, the nitrate family never misses, and the carbonate family mostly stays home.
low.examPointer: Learn the table row by row; each row pairs a soluble majority with a named insoluble exception.

medium.restatement: The rules partition the salt families: sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds and all nitrates are soluble without exception; chlorides and sulfates are soluble except for a few named metals; carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble except for the same soluble trio. The table of record lists each family with its soluble and insoluble members side by side.
medium.analogy: Picture a seating plan where most of each family sits on the soluble side, with a handful of named guests, silver, lead and barium, seated on the insoluble side.
medium.examPointer: Quote both sides of each row: the soluble majority and its exceptions earn the mark together.

check.stem: Which trio of metals gives salts that are always soluble?

options.explanation: Common compounds of these three are soluble with no exceptions listed.
These are exactly the exception names, appearing on the insoluble side of the table.
options.misconception: exception metals mistaken for the soluble trio

options.explanation: Calcium appears only as the slightly soluble hydroxide; none of the three belongs to the always-soluble trio.
These metals are not part of the always-soluble rule.
The nitrate row lists every salt as soluble with no insoluble members.
Silver chloride is the insoluble one; silver nitrate dissolves like every nitrate.

options.text: Three; the heavy-metal nitrates are insoluble
options.explanation: No nitrate exceptions exist in the table of record.
The rules of record are stated without temperature conditions.

check.stem: Which two chlorides are the insoluble exceptions?

options.explanation: These are the two named exceptions in the chloride row.
Both are soluble, belonging to the always-soluble trio.
Barium and calcium are sulfate exceptions, not chloride exceptions.
Ammonium salts are always soluble, and copper chloride is not a listed exception.

check.stem: Which sulfates are named as insoluble?

options.text: Barium sulfate, calcium sulfate and lead(II) sulfate
options.explanation: These three are the sulfate exceptions of record.
Both dissolve; their metals are in the always-soluble trio.
Silver is the chloride exception; the sulfate list names barium, calcium and lead(II).
Most sulfates are soluble; only the three named ones are not.

check.stem: Why does a chemist learn these solubility rules?

options.text: To choose the most appropriate preparation method for a required salt
options.explanation: Whether the target salt dissolves decides how it can be made and collected.

options.text: To decide the colour of the salt
options.explanation: Colour is unrelated to the solubility rules.

options.text: To work out the formula of the salt
options.explanation: Formulae come from ion charges; solubility is about dissolving.

options.text: To measure the strength of the acid used
options.explanation: Acid strength is a separate idea from salt solubility.

lessons.title: Solubility exceptions and limewater
lessons.opening: The exceptions are where marks hide: chlorides of silver and lead(II) will not dissolve, and barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates stay solid. Carbonates and hydroxides only dissolve for sodium, potassium and ammonium, with calcium hydroxide only slightly soluble. That sparingly soluble hydroxide is limewater, the standard test for carbon dioxide gas.
keyPoints: Silver chloride and lead(II) chloride are the insoluble chlorides.
Barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates are the insoluble sulfates.
Carbonates dissolve only for sodium, potassium and ammonium.
Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble in water.
Limewater, calcium hydroxide solution, is the test for carbon dioxide.

low.restatement: Remember the exceptions as short lists: silver and lead(II) among the chlorides; barium, calcium and lead(II) among the sulfates; and only the sodium, potassium and ammonium members among carbonates and hydroxides. Calcium hydroxide, the limewater of the gas tests, is only just soluble.
low.analogy: Exceptions are like a short blacklist at a club door: a few named metals stay outside while everyone else in the family gets in.
low.examPointer: Exception lists are one-mark gold; write them in full rather than as a vague some-metals answer.

medium.restatement: Each soluble family carries named exceptions that examiners quote: silver chloride and lead(II) chloride among the chlorides; barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates among the sulfates. Carbonates and hydroxides invert the pattern, dissolving only for sodium, potassium and ammonium, with calcium hydroxide as the borderline case, sparingly soluble and famous as limewater for the carbon dioxide test.
medium.analogy: Think of the borderline member as the family friend who visits but never stays: calcium hydroxide dissolves a little, enough to make limewater, then stops.
medium.examPointer: Link the exception to the application: knowing barium sulfate is insoluble explains its appearance in precipitation questions.

check.stem: A white precipitate forms when silver nitrate meets a chloride. Why?

options.text: Silver chloride is one of the insoluble chlorides
options.explanation: The solid appearing is silver chloride, the named chloride exception that will not dissolve.
All nitrates are soluble; the solid is the chloride formed.

options.text: The nitrate ions turn solid in water
options.explanation: Nitrate ions never form solids on their own here.
Most chlorides dissolve; only silver and lead(II) do not.

check.stem: Which of these sulfates dissolves in water?

options.explanation: Sodium is in the always-soluble trio, so its sulfate dissolves.
Barium sulfate is a named insoluble exception.
Lead(II) sulfate is on the insoluble list.
Calcium sulfate is the third named sulfate exception.

check.stem: Which carbonate will dissolve in water?

options.explanation: Ammonium is one of the three whose carbonates dissolve.
Copper is not in the soluble trio, so its carbonate is insoluble.
Calcium carbonate, as in limestone and marble, is insoluble.
Iron is not in the soluble trio either.

options.text: A solution of calcium hydroxide, which is only slightly soluble
options.explanation: Limewater is the common name for calcium hydroxide solution, the sparingly soluble hydroxide.
Sodium hydroxide is fully soluble and has its own name; limewater is calcium hydroxide.
Calcium carbonate is insoluble, so it cannot make limewater.
Limewater is a specific substance, not a general term for alkalis.

check.stem: Calcium hydroxide is listed as slightly soluble, while sodium hydroxide is fully soluble. What does this tell you about the hydroxide row?

options.text: The hydroxide family has a borderline member between the soluble trio and the insoluble rest
options.explanation: The row's shape is exactly that: a soluble trio, one sparingly soluble member, and mostly insoluble otherwise.
The contrast in the question itself shows they are not.

options.text: Calcium hydroxide is insoluble in every amount
options.explanation: Slightly soluble means a little dissolves, which is why limewater exists.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide is the only soluble hydroxide
options.explanation: Potassium and ammonium hydroxides dissolve too; calcium is the borderline case.

glossary.definition: How well a substance dissolves in a solvent such as water.
Unable to dissolve in water, so it stays as a solid.
The salt family whose members all dissolve in water.
The salt family soluble except for silver chloride and lead(II) chloride.
The salt family soluble except for barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates.
The salt family insoluble except for sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates.
The salt family insoluble except for sodium, potassium and ammonium, with calcium hydroxide only slightly soluble.

workedExample.prompt: Using the solubility rules, classify each as soluble or insoluble in water: a) potassium carbonate; b) silver chloride; c) barium sulfate; d) ammonium nitrate. e) Which rule makes nitrates convenient starting materials for preparing salts?
steps: a) Soluble: common carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium.
b) Insoluble: common chlorides are soluble except those of silver and lead(II).
c) Insoluble: common sulfates are soluble except those of barium, calcium and lead(II).
d) Soluble: all nitrates dissolve, and all common ammonium compounds are soluble.
e) All nitrates are soluble, so a nitrate of silver or lead(II) can serve as the soluble reactant for precipitating an insoluble salt.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Soluble. b) Insoluble. c) Insoluble. d) Soluble. e) Every nitrate dissolves, so nitrates are universal soluble starting salts.
